title: Hematologic Malignancies: Leukemia, Lymphoma & Multiple Myeloma
html:
Hematologic malignancies can begin in marrow-forming cells, lymphocytes, or plasma cells. The RN does not diagnose a cancer from one blood count, enlarged lymph node, or protein result. Instead, connect the disease location with its physiologic consequences, recognize time-sensitive complications, protect the patient during testing and treatment, and communicate exact trends. Acute leukemia often presents through marrow failure; lymphoma through lymphatic tissue and systemic symptoms; and multiple myeloma through abnormal plasma-cell protein and organ injury.

Learning goals

  • Distinguish leukemia, lymphoma, and multiple myeloma by the cell or tissue involved and the dominant clinical pattern.
  • Recognize infection, anemia, bleeding, leukostasis, hyperviscosity, hypercalcemia, kidney injury, and skeletal emergencies.
  • Explain why definitive classification requires blood, marrow, tissue, imaging, cytogenetic, molecular, and protein studies selected for the suspected disease.
  • Provide safe supportive care during subtype-directed chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, radiation, transplant, or observation.
  • Use serial assessment to determine whether organ function and treatment tolerance are improving.

Start with the cell line and the pattern

Leukemia arises from blood-forming cells and commonly involves marrow and blood. Acute leukemia can crowd out normal hematopoiesis, producing infection risk from ineffective or low neutrophils, fatigue or dyspnea from anemia, and bruising or bleeding from thrombocytopenia. A high white-cell count does not guarantee effective immunity because many circulating cells may be immature or abnormal. Lymphoma arises from lymphocytes and often appears as persistent lymph-node enlargement or extranodal disease. Fever, drenching night sweats, and unintentional weight loss are systemic “B symptoms,” but infection and other conditions remain in the differential. Multiple myeloma is a plasma-cell malignancy that can produce a monoclonal protein and injury to bone, kidneys, marrow, and calcium regulation.

Acute leukemia: marrow failure and abnormal-cell burden

Assess fever, mouth or line changes, dyspnea, fatigue, pallor, petechiae, ecchymoses, mucosal bleeding, and neurologic or respiratory change. Trend the complete blood count with differential, absolute neutrophil count, hemoglobin, platelets, coagulation results, chemistry, kidney function, uric acid, and lactate dehydrogenase in context. Diagnosis and classification commonly require peripheral smear, bone marrow aspiration or biopsy, immunophenotyping, cytogenetic testing, and molecular testing. These results matter because acute myeloid leukemia is not one uniform disease and treatment depends on subtype, fitness, genetic findings, and goals of care.

A very high circulating blast burden with new dyspnea, hypoxemia, headache, confusion, focal deficit, or visual change is an emergency pattern that can represent leukostasis or another critical cause. Escalate immediately, support airway and oxygenation, protect the patient from falls or aspiration, and prepare for specialist-directed cytoreduction and diagnostic evaluation. Do not assume the symptoms are explained by anxiety, anemia, or the laboratory value alone. Fever follows the urgent neutropenic-infection pathway covered in Lesson 102; treatment-associated tumor lysis also requires the electrolyte, rhythm, kidney, and fluid surveillance from that lesson.

Lymphoma: tissue diagnosis before treatment

Evaluate the location, duration, tenderness, texture, and progression of lymph-node enlargement together with fever, drenching night sweats, weight change, pruritus, fatigue, infection history, and extranodal symptoms. Lymphoma may be indolent or aggressive; symptom intensity and node size alone cannot establish subtype. Tissue architecture is important, so an appropriate lymph-node or tissue biopsy is generally central to diagnosis. Imaging, laboratory studies, marrow evaluation in selected cases, and disease-specific staging then define distribution and guide therapy.

Assess for organ compression rather than focusing only on the node. Facial or neck swelling, venous distention, dyspnea, cough, stridor, or difficulty lying flat can signal mediastinal or superior vena cava obstruction. New severe back pain, weakness, sensory loss, gait change, or bladder or bowel dysfunction can indicate spinal cord compression. These findings require urgent escalation, positioning and airway support based on tolerance, focused neurologic assessment, and rapid preparation for ordered imaging and treatment.

Multiple myeloma: remember CRAB, then assess beyond the acronym

The classic organ-injury pattern is Calcium elevation, Renal dysfunction, Anemia, and Bone lesions. Ask about persistent back, rib, or hip pain; reduced height; weakness; constipation; thirst; polyuria; confusion; fatigue; recurrent infection; reduced urine; and medication or contrast exposure. Trend calcium with albumin or the ordered ionized calcium, creatinine and urine output, hemoglobin, protein studies, and imaging. Serum and urine protein testing and serum free light chains help characterize monoclonal protein, while marrow and imaging establish the plasma-cell burden and bone disease.

Protect fragile bone: use safe handling, prescribed mobility support, fall prevention, and prompt evaluation of new focal pain. Do not perform forceful range-of-motion or manipulation over suspected lesions. New weakness, saddle sensory change, or bladder or bowel dysfunction is a spinal emergency. Hypercalcemia can cause dehydration, kidney injury, constipation, weakness, shortened QT, and altered mental status. Follow the ordered hydration and calcium-lowering plan while reassessing lungs, weight, intake and output, rhythm, cognition, and renal function; fluid therapy must be individualized when heart or kidney reserve is limited. Avoid unreviewed nephrotoxic drugs and report falling urine output.

Hyperviscosity and other urgent patterns

Excess monoclonal protein can rarely make plasma more viscous. New headache, dizziness, visual change, somnolence, dyspnea, heart-failure findings, or mucosal oozing in a patient with a paraproteinemia is an emergency pattern. Protect the airway and neurologic safety, notify the oncology team immediately, obtain ordered studies, and prepare for disease-specific treatment such as specialist-directed plasma exchange when indicated. Do not delay escalation while waiting for a single viscosity result. Also prioritize sepsis, major hemorrhage, symptomatic anemia, pathologic fracture, spinal cord compression, acute kidney injury, severe hypercalcemia, and treatment-related tumor lysis.

Treatment is disease- and subtype-specific

Therapy may include combination chemotherapy, monoclonal antibodies, small-molecule targeted therapy, immune therapy, corticosteroids, radiation, stem cell transplant, cellular therapy, or active surveillance for selected indolent disease. Verify the exact diagnosis, regimen, cycle and day, laboratory parameters, prophylaxis, vascular access, premedications, and hold criteria. Monitor infusion reactions, infection, bleeding, mucositis, nausea, bowel change, neuropathy, thrombosis, organ toxicity, and adherence. Supportive care may include antimicrobial prophylaxis, transfusion, growth factors, antiemetics, pain therapy, bone-directed therapy, hydration, kidney protection, nutrition, and fertility or reproductive counseling according to the individualized plan.

Teach patients not to compare regimens solely by the disease name. Molecular findings, stage, symptoms, prior treatment, comorbidities, organ function, and patient goals change the plan. Reinforce the exact fever threshold and emergency number, bleeding precautions when platelets are low, infection prevention, medication and supplement review, oral care, safe activity, hydration instructions, and when new pain or neurologic symptoms require immediate contact.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify the suspected cell line, blood-count pattern, lymph-node or organ findings, B symptoms, CRAB features, pain, neurologic status, urine output, infection and bleeding signs.
  2. Analyze cues: Link cytopenias to marrow failure, distinguish lymphatic mass effects from infection, and connect monoclonal protein or bone disease with kidney, calcium, viscosity, and fracture risk.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Airway compromise, sepsis, leukostasis, hyperviscosity, major bleeding, cord compression, severe hypercalcemia, kidney injury, fracture, and tumor lysis outrank routine education.
  4. Generate solutions: Activate the oncology or emergency pathway, support airway and circulation, obtain ordered cultures and diagnostic studies, protect fragile bone, and prepare disease-specific rescue treatment.
  5. Take action: Escalate exact changes, implement prescribed precautions and therapy, monitor transfusions and infusions, reduce infection and bleeding exposure, and avoid independent treatment based on one value.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess symptoms, mental and neurologic status, oxygenation, bleeding, temperature, blood counts, calcium, kidney function, urine output, pain, mobility, and understanding of the emergency plan.

Clinical example

A patient being evaluated for multiple myeloma reports worsening back pain and constipation. The RN notes increasing confusion, generalized weakness, calcium elevation, rising creatinine, and reduced urine output. Rather than treating constipation as an isolated problem, the RN recognizes a hypercalcemia-and-kidney-injury pattern, urgently notifies the oncology team, begins ordered monitoring and individualized fluid therapy, reviews nephrotoxic exposure, institutes fall and bone precautions, and performs a focused neurologic assessment. New leg weakness or bladder dysfunction would trigger immediate spinal cord compression evaluation.
